codecov:
    # Uploads what the test job saved, from a job of its own, so the OIDC
    # token that signs in to Codecov never exists beside the install and the
    # tests. The checkout, which keeps no token, is there only so Codecov can
    # match report paths to files: the job installs nothing and runs none of
    # the repository's code. It runs whenever the test job ran, failures
    # included, so failing tests still reach Codecov, and only on the events
    # that collect coverage. A run the concurrency group cancels uploads
    # nothing, and each run reads only its own artifacts.
    needs: lint-test-build
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.lint-test-build.result != 'cancelled' && needs.lint-test-build.result != 'skipped' && (github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.ref == format('refs/heads/{0}', github.event.repository.default_branch)) }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      # Each artifact unpacks where the test job wrote its files. A pattern
      # that matches nothing, unlike a name, does not fail: a failing test
      # run saves test results and no coverage.
      - name: Download coverage
        uses: actions/download-artifact@3e5f45b2cfb9172054b4087a40e8e0b5a5461e7c # v8.0.1
        with:
          pattern: codecov-coverage
          path: coverage
      - name: Download test results
        uses: actions/download-artifact@3e5f45b2cfb9172054b4087a40e8e0b5a5461e7c # v8.0.1
        with:
          pattern: codecov-test-results
          path: .
      # After a passing test job both artifacts exist, so each upload runs,
      # and fails the job if its files are missing; after a failing one each
      # runs when its files arrived. Both sign in with OIDC, fail the job when
      # Codecov refuses the report, and run the Codecov CLI at a fixed version
      # rather than whichever is newest.
      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        if: ${{ needs.lint-test-build.result == 'success' || hashFiles('coverage/lcov.info') != '' }}
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@303a32d7a59b442fa8d48b6a1cc6825c09c847a5 # v7.1.1
        with:
          version: v11.3.1
          use_oidc: true
          fail_ci_if_error: true
          disable_search: true
          files: ./coverage/lcov.info
      - name: Upload test results to Codecov
        if: ${{ needs.lint-test-build.result == 'success' || hashFiles('junit.xml') != '' }}
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@303a32d7a59b442fa8d48b6a1cc6825c09c847a5 # v7.1.1
        with:
          version: v11.3.1
          use_oidc: true
          fail_ci_if_error: true
          report_type: test_results
          disable_search: true
          files: ./junit.xml

Node 20 in the `lint-test-build` matrix fails the range that `package-lock.json` declares for vitest. The job runs the tests with `npm test` and `npm run test:ci`.

The lock file has vitest 5.0.0 with `engines.node` set to `^22.12.0 || ^24.0.0 || >=26.0.0`. The matrix at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:80` is `node-version: [20, 22, 24]`, so only the 20 leg falls outside that range. I did not run the workflow.

Node 22 and 24 satisfy the range. The other tool I checked, vite 8.2.2, declares `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`. That allows Node 20 only from 20.19.0, and the matrix pins just the major version, so I treated it as not the mismatch.

```json
{"file": ".github/workflows/ci.yml", "job": "lint-test-build", "line": 80, "node": "20", "tool": "vitest", "requires": "^22.12.0 || ^24.0.0 || >=26.0.0"}
```

content.text:
1. Time and cost: Two things cost me the most. One Bash call failed because it contained a pipe to `sort` and another used shell arithmetic. I also had to read the lock file in pieces to work out which package owned each `engines.node` line. A single query that listed each package's name, version and engines range together would have saved the most. The workflow itself was easy to read.

2. Clarity: "Test tool" could have meant vitest, vite or something else. I took vitest because the job calls `npm test` and `npm run test:ci`, and its range was the only one that excluded a pinned Node version. "The line" could have meant the matrix line or the `setup-node` line. I chose line 80, where the version is pinned in the `[20, 22, 24]` matrix. The "Node version pinned" is also a bare major, "20", so I gave that.

3. Tools: I relied on Bash with grep and sed, plus a couple of file reads. Grep and Read were the tools I should have used for those tasks. I wanted a lock-file-aware query. I didn't run the Grep tool at all. Nothing misled me, but a bare `"node":` grep returned many unrelated lines, such as commander's `>=22.12.0`. I never confirmed what `package.json` scripts run. The workflow's comment that Atlas needs Node 22 is true, but it is about a different tool.

4. Confidence: I'm fairly confident, around 85%. The vitest range and the matrix entry are both directly visible, and the range excludes 20. I would have checked three things next: the `package.json` `engines` and scripts, whether `test:ci` really invokes vitest, and whether another lock entry for a test-related tool (for example a coverage package) also conflicts with 20. I'm least sure of my reading of `@vitest/istanbul-lib-coverage` at `>=22`. I didn't verify it is used in the Node 20 leg, and I only inferred that the `COVERAGE_LEG` step runs on 22. If the intended tool was that coverage package, my answer is wrong.

5. Future development: A tool that resolves "which packages in the lock file conflict with this Node version" would remove most of the manual work. For this kind of task, the question could say whether "test tool" means the runner or any package. It could also say which line to report when a version is set in a matrix.
